claim: Unesterified cholesterol accumulation in the late endosomal/lysosomal (LE/LY) compartment is the cellular hallmark of Niemann-Pick C (NPC) disease.
source: Unesterified cholesterol accumulation in the late endosomal/lysosomal (LE/LY) compartment is the cellular hallmark of Niemann-Pick C (NPC) disease, caused by defects in the genes encoding NPC1 or NPC2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPC disease and is supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: NPC disease is caused by defects in the genes encoding NPC1 or NPC2.
source: Unesterified cholesterol accumulation in the late endosomal/lysosomal (LE/LY) compartment is the cellular hallmark of Niemann-Pick C (NPC) disease, caused by defects in the genes encoding NPC1 or NPC2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic basis of NPC disease.

claim: LBPA dramatically stimulates NPC2 cholesterol transport rates to and from model membranes.
source: We previously reported the dramatic stimulation of NPC2 cholesterol transport rates to and from model membranes by the LE/LY phospholipid lysobisphosphatidic acid (LBPA).
evidence: This claim references previous work by the authors and is supported by citation to their prior studies.

claim: Enrichment of NPC1-deficient cells with LBPA results in cholesterol clearance.
source: It had been previously shown that enrichment of NPC1-deficient cells with LBPA results in cholesterol clearance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Chevallier et al., 2008).

claim: LBPA enrichment in human NPC2-deficient cells is entirely ineffective at clearing cholesterol.
source: Here we demonstrate that LBPA enrichment in human NPC2-deficient cells, either directly or via its biosynthetic precursor phosphtidylglycerol (PG), is entirely ineffective, indicating an obligate functional interaction between NPC2 and LBPA in cholesterol trafficking.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 8).

claim: There is an obligate functional interaction between NPC2 and LBPA in cholesterol trafficking.
source: Here we demonstrate that LBPA enrichment in human NPC2-deficient cells, either directly or via its biosynthetic precursor phosphtidylglycerol (PG), is entirely ineffective, indicating an obligate functional interaction between NPC2 and LBPA in cholesterol trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that LBPA enrichment is ineffective in NPC2-deficient cells.

claim: NPC2 interacts directly with LBPA.
source: We further demonstrate that NPC2 interacts directly with LBPA and identify the NPC2 hydrophobic knob domain as the site of interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays and HTRF analysis (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: The NPC2 hydrophobic knob domain is the site of interaction with LBPA.
source: We further demonstrate that NPC2 interacts directly with LBPA and identify the NPC2 hydrophobic knob domain as the site of interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis studies showing that mutations in the hydrophobic knob reduce LBPA binding (Figure 5).

claim: Intracellular cholesterol trafficking is critically dependent upon the interaction of LBPA with functional NPC2 protein.
source: Together these studies reveal a heretofore unknown step of intracellular cholesterol trafficking which is critically dependent upon the interaction of LBPA with functional NPC2 protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that LBPA enrichment requires functional NPC2 to clear cholesterol.

claim: In 95% of NPC cases, mutations in NPC1 prevent proper export of cholesterol from the LE/LY to other cellular compartments.
source: In 95% of NPC cases, mutations in the large LE/LY transmembrane protein, NPC1, prevent proper export of cholesterol from the LE/LY to other cellular compartments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the prevalence of NPC1 mutations in NPC disease.

claim: The remaining 5% of NPC cases are caused by mutations in NPC2.
source: The remaining 5% of cases are caused by mutations in the small, 132-amino acid, soluble LE/LY protein, NPC2 (Peake and Vance, 2010; Vanier, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to the literature.

claim: NPC2 is a small, 132-amino acid, soluble LE/LY protein.
source: The remaining 5% of cases are caused by mutations in the small, 132-amino acid, soluble LE/LY protein, NPC2 (Peake and Vance, 2010; Vanier, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the characteristics of NPC2 protein.

claim: NPC1 and NPC2 function cooperatively in normal LE/LY cholesterol trafficking.
source: Similarities in the cellular and clinical phenotypes resulting from either NPC1 or NPC2 deficiency led to the suggestion that these two proteins function cooperatively in normal LE/LY cholesterol trafficking (Kwon et al., 2009; Sleat et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A proposed model shows cholesterol directly transferred from NPC2 to NPC1.
source: a proposed model shows cholesterol directly transferred from NPC2, in the LE/LY lumen, to NPC1, located in the limiting membrane of the compartment (Estiu et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature proposing this model.

claim: NPC2 binds cholesterol with a 1:1 stoichiometry.
source: NPC2 binds cholesterol with a 1:1 stoichiometry (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol binding by NPC2 is necessary but not sufficient for its cholesterol efflux function.
source: Ko et al. (2003) showed that cholesterol binding was necessary but not sufficient for its cholesterol efflux function
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol transport is a critical component of NPC2 functionality.
source: we later demonstrated that cholesterol transport was the second critical component of NPC2 functionality (Cheruku et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Cholesterol transfer by NPC2 occurs via protein-membrane interactions.
source: We further showed that cholesterol transfer by NPC2 occurs via protein-membrane interactions (Cheruku et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: LBPA is localized primarily to inner LE/LY membranes.
source: LBPA is a structural isomer of phosphatidylglyerol with an atypical phospholipid stereoconfiguration. It is localized primarily to inner LE/LY membranes and is thought to be involved not only in the formation of these internal membranes and their architecture, but also in the sorting and efflux of LE/LY components, including cholesterol (Gruenberg, 2003; Hullin-Matsuda et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 1998; Kobayashi et al., 1999; Möbius et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LBPA is thought to be involved in the formation of internal LE/LY membranes and their architecture.
source: It is localized primarily to inner LE/LY membranes and is thought to be involved not only in the formation of these internal membranes and their architecture, but also in the sorting and efflux of LE/LY components, including cholesterol (Gruenberg, 2003; Hullin-Matsuda et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 1998; Kobayashi et al., 1999; Möbius et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LBPA is thought to be involved in the sorting and efflux of LE/LY components, including cholesterol.
source: It is localized primarily to inner LE/LY membranes and is thought to be involved not only in the formation of these internal membranes and their architecture, but also in the sorting and efflux of LE/LY components, including cholesterol (Gruenberg, 2003; Hullin-Matsuda et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 1998; Kobayashi et al., 1999; Möbius et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Incubation of BHK cells and macrophages with an anti-LBPA monoclonal antibody results in cholesterol accumulation in the LE/LY compartment, resembling the NPC phenotype.
source: Incubation of BHK cells and macrophages with an anti-LBPA monoclonal antibody results in cholesterol accumulation in the LE/LY compartment, resembling the NPC phenotype (Delton-Vandenbroucke et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Chevallier et al. (2008) showed that by enriching NPC1-deficient cells with exogenously added LBPA, the cholesterol accumulation was reversed.
source: Interestingly, Chevallier et al. (2008) showed that by enriching NPC1-deficient cells with exogenously added LBPA, the cholesterol accumulation was reversed
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The underlying molecular mechanism for LBPA stimulated LE/LY cholesterol egress remains unknown.
source: the underlying molecular mechanism for LBPA stimulated LE/LY cholesterol egress remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The OPM database predicts that a loop domain consisting of hydrophobic residues 56-HGIVMGIPV-64 on NPC2 is highly membrane interactive, with a ΔG of −4.6 kcal/mol.
source: Using the crystal structure of bovine NPC2 (PDB ID: 1NEP), a loop domain consisting of hydrophobic residues as highlighted in Figure 1 was predicted to be highly membrane interactive, with a ΔG of −4.6 kcal/mol. This domain corresponds to 56-HGIVMGIPV-64
evidence: This claim is based on computational predictions from the OPM database using the crystal structure of NPC2.

claim: The hydrophobic knob domain forms a prominent structure on the surface of the NPC2 protein.
source: Structurally, this domain forms a hydrophobic knob which presents prominently on the surface of the NPC2 protein.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the NPC2 protein.

claim: OPM predicts that the hydrophobic knob domain inserts into the hydrophobic space of the membrane model, positioning the sterol binding pocket of NPC2 near the membrane surface.
source: OPM predicts that this knob domain inserts into the hydrophobic space of the membrane model, positioning the sterol binding pocket of NPC2 near the membrane surface (Figure 1A)
evidence: This claim is based on computational predictions from the OPM database.

claim: The primary sequence of the hydrophobic knob domain is conserved in mammalian NPC2 proteins but not in the yeast NPC2 homologue.
source: Of note, and as shown in Figure 1B, the primary sequence of the hydrophobic knob domain is conserved in mammalian NPC2 proteins but not in the yeast NPC2 homologue.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The hydrophobicity of the knob domain is conserved amongst mammalian NPC2 proteins, in contrast to the low hydrophobicity in the yeast NPC2 protein.
source: Hydrophobicity scales for NPC2 as well as a Kyte-Doolittle plot of the hydrophobicity scores along the primary protein sequence indicate that the hydrophobicity of the knob domain is conserved amongst mammalian NPC2 proteins, in contrast to the low hydrophobicity in the yeast NPC2 protein (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrophobicity analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Increasing the mol% of LBPA in SUV from 0% to 30% increases NPC2 cholesterol transfer rates by approximately 100 fold.
source: The results in Figure 2 indicate an exponential relationship between the LBPA content of the vesicles and the NPC2 cholesterol transfer rate; increasing the mol% of LBPA in SUV from 0% to 30% effectively increases the NPC2 cholesterol transfer rates by approximately 100 fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is an exponential relationship between the LBPA content of vesicles and the NPC2 cholesterol transfer rate.
source: The results in Figure 2 indicate an exponential relationship between the LBPA content of the vesicles and the NPC2 cholesterol transfer rate
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The relative partition of cholesterol between NPC2 and phospholipid vesicles is >30:1, mol NPC2:mol PL.
source: The results showed that the labeled cholesterol transfers from NPC2 to membranes and from membranes to NPC2, and in agreement with previous experiments using tryptophan quenching to determine sterol distribution, the relative partition of cholesterol between NPC2 and phospholipid vesicles was >30:1, mol NPC2:mol PL (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using 3H-cholesterol and is consistent with previous work.

claim: No appreciable differences in the equilibrium distribution of cholesterol between NPC2 and different membranes (EPC vs LBPA-containing) were found.
source: Although there is order of magnitude more rapid sterol transfer from NPC2 to LBPA-containing vesicles relative to EPC vesicles, no appreciable differences in the equilibrium distribution of cholesterol between NPC2 and the different membranes were found.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from the 3H-cholesterol transfer experiments.

claim: Point mutations in multiple regions on the NPC2 surface, including in the hydrophobic knob domain, led to diminished rates of cholesterol transfer between NPC2 and zwitterionic PC membranes.
source: Using zwitterionic PC membranes we recently reported that point mutations in multiple regions on the NPC2 surface, including in the hydrophobic knob domain, led to diminished rates of cholesterol transfer between NPC2 and membranes (McCauliff et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: When acceptor membranes included 25 mol% of LBPA, cholesterol transfer rates for NPC2 proteins with mutations in regions other than the hydrophobic knob were similar to those of WT.
source: The results in Figure 3A show that when acceptor membranes included 25 mol% of LBPA, cholesterol transfer rates for NPC2 proteins with mutations in regions other than the hydrophobic knob were similar to those of WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mutations at H31, Q29, D113, and E108 exhibited sterol transfer rates to zwitterionic EPC membranes that were ≤15% of WT NPC2.
source: Surprisingly, though mutations at H31, Q29, D113, and E108 exhibited sterol transfer rates to zwitterionic EPC membranes that were ≤15% of WT NPC2, the inclusion of LBPA in acceptor membranes resulted in rates of cholesterol transfer that were ≥85% of WT rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The inclusion of LBPA in acceptor membranes resulted in rates of cholesterol transfer by H31, Q29, D113, and E108 mutants that were ≥85% of WT rates.
source: Surprisingly, though mutations at H31, Q29, D113, and E108 exhibited sterol transfer rates to zwitterionic EPC membranes that were ≤15% of WT NPC2, the inclusion of LBPA in acceptor membranes resulted in rates of cholesterol transfer that were ≥85% of WT rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The I62 and V64 mutations resulted in markedly defective cholesterol transfer to EPC vesicles and were unaffected by the inclusion of LBPA in the acceptor membranes.
source: By contrast the I62 and V64 mutations, both in the hydrophobic knob and which also resulted in markedly defective cholesterol transfer to EPC vesicles, were unaffected by the inclusion of LBPA in the acceptor membranes, with cholesterol transfer by these mutants remaining barely detectable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The G61A mutation resulted in cholesterol transfer deficiencies similar to the I62 and V64 mutants, with sterol transfer to EPC vesicles reduced by 70%.
source: The G61A mutation, also in the hydrophobic knob, resulted in cholesterol transfer deficiencies similar to the I62 and V64 mutants, though changes are less extreme; sterol transfer to EPC vesicles was reduced by 70%, and it remained highly defective in the presence of LBPA, with rates of cholesterol transfer of only 16% relative to WT NPC2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mutations in hydrophobic knob residues H56, G57, and I58 had little effect on cholesterol transfer rates to EPC vesicles.
source: Mutations in hydrophobic knob residues H56, G57, and I58 had little effect on cholesterol transfer rates to EPC vesicles, however unlike the WT NPC2, these mutants were insensitive to the presence of LBPA in acceptor membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: H56, G57, and I58 mutants were insensitive to the presence of LBPA in acceptor membranes.
source: Mutations in hydrophobic knob residues H56, G57, and I58 had little effect on cholesterol transfer rates to EPC vesicles, however unlike the WT NPC2, these mutants were insensitive to the presence of LBPA in acceptor membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The mutations which remained insensitive to membrane LBPA were localized exclusively in the hydrophobic knob domain.
source: In striking contrast, Figure 3C shows that the mutations which remained insensitive to membrane LBPA (shown in red) were localized exclusively in the hydrophobic knob domain
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and structural mapping shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The hydrophobic knob domain is the sole LBPA-sensitive region on the protein surface.
source: These results strongly indicate that the hydrophobic knob domain is the sole LBPA-sensitive region on the protein surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that only mutations in the hydrophobic knob affect LBPA sensitivity.

claim: WT NPC2 promotes membrane-membrane interactions.
source: We and others have shown that WT NPC2 promotes membrane-membrane interactions (Abdul-Hammed et al., 2010; Berzina et al., 2018; McCauliff et al., 2011; McCauliff et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature including the authors' own work.

claim: NPC2 point mutants with deficient cholesterol transfer abilities are unable to cause EPC membrane aggregation.
source: We further showed that NPC2 point mutants with deficient cholesterol transfer abilities are also unable to cause EPC membrane aggregation (McCauliff et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Inclusion of 25 mol% LBPA in LUVs resulted in a 16-fold increase in the rate of membrane-membrane interaction by WT NPC2, relative to 100% EPC LUVs.
source: The results in Table 1 show that inclusion of 25 mol% LBPA in LUVs resulted in a 16-fold increase in the rate of membrane-membrane interaction by WT NPC2, relative to 100% EPC LUVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Incorporation of LBPA into membranes normalizes the membrane aggregation rates for NPC2 proteins with mutations outside the hydrophobic knob.
source: Incorporation of LBPA into membranes normalizes the membrane aggregation rates for NPC2 proteins with mutations outside the hydrophobic knob, for example H31, D113, and Q29.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Hydrophobic knob domain mutations were relatively insensitive to membrane LBPA in membrane aggregation assays.
source: By contrast, the hydrophobic knob domain mutations were relatively insensitive to membrane LBPA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: WT NPC2 binds to LBPA.
source: The results shown in Figure 4A demonstrate that WT NPC2 binds to LBPA
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: WT NPC2 shows greater interaction with LBPA isomers containing oleoyl (C18:1) as opposed to myristoyl (C14:0) fatty acyl chains.
source: The results shown in Figure 4A demonstrate that WT NPC2 binds to LBPA, showing greater interaction with isomers containing oleoyl (C18:1) as opposed to myristoyl (C14:0) fatty acyl chains
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: WT NPC2 shows the greatest degree of binding to the S,S 18:1 LBPA.
source: and overall the greatest degree of binding to the S,S 18:1 LBPA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NPC2 binding to S,S 18:1 LBPA was greater than binding to egg PC.
source: NPC2 binding to S,S 18:1 LBPA was also greater than binding to egg PC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NPC2 interacts more strongly with LBPA than with PC, PA, PG, and PS species.
source: Figure 4B shows that NPC2 interacts more strongly with LBPA than with PC, PA, PG, and PS species.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mechanism by which NPC2 binds to LBPA is likely not solely dependent on electrostatic interactions.
source: As two other anionic phospholipids assayed, PG and PA, show even less interaction with NPC2 than does zwitterionic PC, the mechanism by which NPC2 binds to LBPA is likely not solely dependent on electrostatic interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NPC2 binds more strongly to LBPA than to other anionic phospholipids.

claim: The NPC2-interaction with LBPA at pH 5.0 was substantially greater than with other negatively charged lipids or with zwitterionic PC.
source: The NPC2-interaction with LBPA at pH 5.0 was substantially greater than with other negatively charged lipids or with zwitterionic PC (Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from HTRF assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mutations in most of the hydrophobic knob residues markedly reduce interactions with LBPA, relative to WT NPC2.
source: The results show that mutations in most of the hydrophobic knob residues markedly reduce interactions, relative to WT NPC2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: The hydrophobic knob mutants I62N and V64A bound the S,S and S,R di-oleoyl isomers at only ~20% of WT levels.
source: For example, studies analyzing binding to various isomers of LBPA show that the hydrophobic knob mutants I62N and V64A bound the S,S and S,R di-oleoyl isomers at only ~20% of WT levels
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Q29A and D113A mutants bound nearly all LBPA isomers similar to WT.
source: In contrast, the Q29A and D113A mutants, in regions outside the hydrophobic knob, bound nearly all LBPA isomers similar to WT
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutations within the hydrophobic knob domain of NPC2 resulted in diminished binding of the protein to LBPA.
source: Overall, mutations within the hydrophobic knob domain of NPC2 resulted in diminished binding of the protein to LBPA while mutations outside the knob region presented proteins with LBPA interactions similar to WT (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mutations outside the knob region presented proteins with LBPA interactions similar to WT.
source: Overall, mutations within the hydrophobic knob domain of NPC2 resulted in diminished binding of the protein to LBPA while mutations outside the knob region presented proteins with LBPA interactions similar to WT (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid blot assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Incubation of NPC2 deficient fibroblasts with WT NPC2 protein resulted in a dramatic decrease in filipin staining, reaching levels similar to healthy fibroblasts.
source: In agreement with several previous reports, incubation of NPC2 deficient fibroblasts with WT NPC2 protein resulted in a dramatic decrease in filipin staining, reaching levels similar to healthy fibroblasts (Figure 6) (Ko et al., 2003; Liou et al., 2006; McCauliff et al., 2011; McCauliff et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and citations to previous literature.

claim: The H56A mutant reduced filipin stain area similar to WT NPC2.
source: The H56A mutant, with rates of sterol transfer and membrane aggregation similar to WT protein, also reduced filipin stain area, similar to WT NPC2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The G57D and I58A hydrophobic knob mutants were unable to reverse cholesterol accumulation in NPC2 cells.
source: In contrast, the G57D and I58A hydrophobic knob mutants, with markedly attenuated cholesterol transfer and membrane aggregation rates, were unable to reverse cholesterol accumulation in NPC2 cells; filipin staining remained at a level comparable to that of the unsupplemented cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: G61A was able to lessen cholesterol accumulation in NPC2 cells to a moderate extent.
source: G61A, also in the knob domain, was able to lessen cholesterol accumulation in NPC2 cells to a moderate extent, and its defect in cholesterol transfer was also more modest than that of other hydrophobic knob mutants (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Incubation of cells with 100% PG SUVs led to substantial increases in cellular content of LBPA in all fibroblast types.
source: The results in Figure 7 show that incubation of the cells with 100% PG SUVs led to substantial increases in cellular content of LBPA in all fibroblast types
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In WT cells, PG supplementation resulted in a nearly 6-fold increase in LBPA.
source: in WT cells the increase was nearly 6-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: LBPA levels in NPC patient cells were found to be increased relative to WT cells prior to enrichment.
source: In agreement with previous reports LBPA levels in NPC patient cells were found to be increased relative to WT cells prior to enrichment (Chevallier et al., 2008; Davidson et al., 2009; Sleat et al., 2004; Vanier, 1983)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: PG incubation resulted in 2–3 fold increases in LBPA in NPC1- and NPC2-deficient cells, respectively, relative to unsupplemented cells.
source: PG incubation resulted in 2–3 fold increases in NPC1- and NPC2-deficient cells, respectively, relative to unsupplemented cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Levels of other cellular phospholipids appeared unchanged after PG supplementation.
source: Levels of other cellular phospholipids appeared unchanged (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Direct addition of LBPA-containing SUVs led to approximately 2 to 3-fold increases in cellular LBPA levels.
source: Direct addition of LBPA-containing SUVs also led to approximately 2 to 3-fold increases in cellular LBPA levels (data not shown), in agreement with (Chevallier et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous literature.

claim: Following PG supplementation, cholesterol content remained unchanged in the WT fibroblasts.
source: Following PG supplementation, cholesterol content remained unchanged in the WT fibroblasts (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: NPC1 deficient fibroblasts exhibited a dramatic reduction in cholesterol accumulation following PG supplementation, approaching levels observed for WT cells.
source: NPC1 deficient fibroblasts exhibited a dramatic reduction in cholesterol accumulation following PG supplementation, approaching levels observed for WT cells and similar to the direct addition of LBPA (Chevallier et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 and citation to previous literature.

claim: The cholesterol accumulation in NPC2 deficient fibroblast remained elevated following PG supplementation, despite increased LBPA content.
source: In marked contrast to NPC1 deficient cells, the cholesterol accumulation in NPC2 deficient fibroblast remained elevated following PG supplementation, despite increased LBPA content (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: PG supplementation led to significant reductions in the cholesterol accumulation phenotype in NPC1 null HeLa cells generated via CRISPR-Cas9.
source: To address this possibility, we generated NPC1 null HeLa cells via CRISPR-Cas9 and found that PG supplementation led to significant reductions in the cholesterol accumulation phenotype (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: In WT cells treated with U18666A, PG supplementation resulted in cholesterol clearance.
source: We additionally performed PG supplementation in WT cells treated with the U18666A compound, known to induce the NPC disease phenotype at the cellular level by targeting NPC1 (Lu et al., 2015). In these cells too, PG supplementation resulted in cholesterol clearance (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and citation to previous literature.

claim: LBPA can promote cholesterol egress from the endolysosomal compartment despite the absence of NPC1, but not in the absence of NPC2.
source: Overall, these results suggest that LBPA can promote cholesterol egress from the endolysosomal compartment despite the absence of NPC1, but not in the absence of NPC2.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations that PG/LBPA supplementation clears cholesterol in NPC1-deficient cells but not in NPC2-deficient cells.

claim: There is a direct relationship between the cholesterol transfer rate of a particular NPC2 mutant and its ability to rescue the cholesterol accumulation of NPC2-deficient cells.
source: The point mutagenesis analysis of NPC2 shows a direct relationship between the cholesterol transfer rate of a particular NPC2 mutant and its ability to rescue the cholesterol accumulation of NPC2-deficient cells (McCauliff et al., 2015; Figures 3 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 6 and citation to previous work.

claim: NPC2 proteins with mutations outside the hydrophobic knob that were unable to reduce cholesterol accumulation in unsupplemented NPC2 deficient cells were able to 'rescue' cells that were enriched with LBPA via PG supplementation.
source: The results in Figure 9 demonstrate that NPC2 proteins with mutations outside the hydrophobic knob, such as Q29A, D113A, and D72A, which were unable to reduce cholesterol accumulation in unsupplemented NPC2 deficient cells, were indeed able to 'rescue' cells that were enriched with LBPA via PG supplementation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The hydrophobic knob mutants I62D and G61A were unable to clear cholesterol from LBPA-enriched NPC2 deficient cells.
source: By contrast, the hydrophobic knob mutants I62D and G61A, which were insensitive to LBPA in cholesterol transfer assays, were unable to clear cholesterol from LBPA-enriched NPC2 deficient cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: A combination of increased cellular levels of LBPA and LBPA-sensitive NPC2 protein was able to rescue the NPC2 deficient cells, beyond the ability of the mutant protein alone.
source: Thus, the results show that a combination of increased cellular levels of LBPA and LBPA-sensitive NPC2 protein was able to rescue the NPC2 deficient cells, beyond the ability of the mutant protein alone (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: LBPA function in cholesterol trafficking is obligately dependent upon its interaction with the NPC2 protein within the endo-lysosomal system.
source: In this study we have, for the first time, shown that LBPA function in cholesterol trafficking is obligately dependent upon its interaction with the NPC2 protein within the endo-lysosomal system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that LBPA enrichment requires functional NPC2 to clear cholesterol.

claim: This novel step in intracellular cholesterol trafficking involves direct interaction of LBPA with the hydrophobic knob domain on NPC2.
source: At the molecular level, we show that this novel step in intracellular cholesterol trafficking involves direct interaction of LBPA with the hydrophobic knob domain on NPC2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from lipid binding assays and mutagenesis studies.

claim: The hydrophobic knob domain is located near the cholesterol binding pocket.
source: This surface domain is located near the cholesterol binding pocket, thus its insertion into the bilayer would position the protein to efficiently exchange cholesterol with the membrane.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the NPC2 protein.

claim: LBPA, but not other phospholipids, may position NPC2 in an orientation that could promote protein-membrane sterol exchange.
source: Recent molecular dynamic simulations show that LBPA, but not other phospholipids, may position NPC2 in an orientation that could promote protein-membrane sterol exchange (Enkavi et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: LBPA enrichment is completely ineffective in cells expressing NPC1 but lacking NPC2.
source: Here we show that LBPA enrichment is, conversely, completely ineffective in cells expressing NPC1 but lacking NPC2, underscoring the required functional interaction of LBPA with the NPC2 protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: LBPA is able to normalize deficient transfer by mutant NPC2 as long as the mutation is outside of the hydrophobic knob.
source: Thus, LBPA is able to normalize deficient transfer by mutant NPC2 as long as the mutation is outside of the hydrophobic knob.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cholesterol transfer assays and cell rescue experiments.

claim: Direct interaction between NPC2 and NPC1 involves the hydrophobic knob region on NPC2.
source: Interestingly, direct interaction between NPC2 and NPC1, residing in the limiting LE/LY membrane, has also been identified as involving the hydrophobic knob region on NPC2 (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The NPC2 hydrophobic knob is involved in both LBPA-dependent binding of cholesterol by NPC2 at inner-LE/LY membranes, and the delivery of cholesterol by NPC2 to the NPC1 N-terminal domain.
source: Thus, we propose that the hydrophobic knob on NPC2 interacts with LBPA in the inner LE/LY membranes, leading to cholesterol extraction, with NPC2 then subsequently involved in the 'handoff' of the sterol to NPC1 in the limiting membrane of these organelles (Deffieu and Pfeffer, 2011; Infante et al., 2008; Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and previous literature.

claim: Yeast lacks the LBPA phospholipid.
source: interestingly, yeast lacks the LBPA phospholipid, indirectly supporting a functional interaction between the mammalian NPC2 hydrophobic knob and LBPA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast lipid composition.

claim: The enrichment of inner LE/LY membranes with LBPA and concurrent decline in cholesterol content may be reflective of the efficient role LBPA plays in normal LE/LY cholesterol efflux.
source: In healthy cells, the enrichment of inner LE/LY membranes with LBPA and concurrent decline in cholesterol content may be reflective of the efficient role LBPA plays in normal LE/LY cholesterol efflux.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed lipid distributions in healthy cells.

claim: LBPA comprises only 1% of total cellular phospholipids.

claim: LBPA comprises about 15 mol% of total phospholipids in the LE/LY.
